case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's reasonable-efforts provision, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries under the Act itself or under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
key_cases.relevance: Suter is the controlling authority that federal compliance failures under Title IV-E are remedied by funding sanctions and corrective action plans, not private damages.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

key_cases.case_name: White Ex Rel. White v. Chambliss
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held South Carolina DSS officials were entitled to qualified immunity on claims arising from the removal of children and the foster placement in which one child died, because no clearly established federal right — including any right created by the South Carolina Child Protection Act — was violated.
key_cases.relevance: White expressly holds the South Carolina Child Protection Act creates no substantive federal right enforceable under § 1983.
key_cases.quote: The facts presented by White reveal that the DSS defendants violated no "clearly established" law in removing White's children from her custody.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a child protection agency to protect a child from violence by a private actor, so the agency's failure to remove the child was not a constitutional violation.
key_cases.relevance: A state's failure to meet child-welfare performance standards is not, without more, a due process violation under DeShaney; the remedy lies in federal funding mechanisms.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors
